find: Binary search also assumes the data lives in a structure that supports random access, where any index can be inspected in constant time. Arrays satisfy this requirement, but linked lists do not — reaching the middle of a linked list itself takes linear time, which cancels the algorithm’s headline advantage. When the spec asks why binary search is unsuitable in a particular scenario, an answer that mentions either “the data is unsorted” or “the structure does not allow random access” will earn the mark.
replace: Binary search also assumes you can jump straight to any position in the data. An array lets you do that, because you can read any index directly. If a question asks why binary search is unsuitable in a scenario, the reason is almost always that the data is not sorted.
note: F11: linked lists are not in the spec's data structures, and the 'will earn the mark' claim is invented.
